findings.evidence: p.59 (Ch 4, Table 4-1, Economic constraints row): Cell status label: "[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] 2026 list-price snapshot, not a procured quote." The cell body contains: "at the ~6-host average the whole-fleet spend is ~$120/hour over the ~173.3 active hours/month (8 h × 260 workdays ÷ 12 = 173.3 h/mo; = $20,800/month), giving ~2.76M input and ~90K output tokens per $1 of fleet spend"
findings.issue: Cell-level label mismatch: the status tag is [ASSUMPTION] but most values in the cell are arithmetic results (173.3 h/mo = 8×260÷12, $20,800 = 120×173.3, 2.76M = 92,000÷0.0333) which the convention (p.17, Table 4-2 note) classifies as [DERIVED], not [ASSUMPTION]. The [ASSUMPTION] tag correctly applies to the price snapshot and schedule inputs, but a reader applying the cell-level tag to derived outputs (173.3, $20,800, 2.76M) would mislabel them.
findings.fix_instruction: Split the cell label to cover both: mark the input components (price, schedule) as [ASSUMPTION] and add a note that derived values within the cell carry [canonical scenario][DERIVED] per the Table-level provenance convention stated in the derivation note beneath the table.

findings.evidence: At the ~6-host average the whole-fleet spend is ~$120/hour ... giving ~2.76M input and ~90K output tokens per $1 of fleet spend (active-hours basis). ... on the 730-hour paid-occupancy basis ($87,600/month ÷ the same month's ~57.4B input tokens) the same fleet yields ~655K input tokens per $1
findings.issue: Two tokens-per-dollar figures for the same fleet and the same token volume coexist with no in-line denominator rule at the point of use, and both are labeled [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]-family values in Table 4-1's Economic row. The book elsewhere (Ch. 4 §4.3, 'Throughput per dollar') explains that the two differ only by the hour-count divisor, but the Canonical Workload box (Table 4-1 row) presents both without an explicit 'do not compare' flag adjacent to the second number. Check: $120/hr ÷ $1/hr = 120 dollars per hour; 92,000 tok/s × 3,600 = 331.2M input tokens/hr → 331.2M/120 = 2.76M tokens/$ ✓. On the 730-hour basis: 6 hosts × 730 h × $20 = $87,600; monthly input tokens = 92,000 × 3,600 × 730 = 241.9B, not the '~57.4B' quoted in the table. 57.4B is instead 331.2M × 173.3 = 57.4B (active hours) — i.e. the table's own parenthetical labels the 730-hour denominator against a 173.3-hour token volume. The numerator/denominator pairing in that cell is internally mislabeled.
findings.fix_instruction: Fix the parenthetical in Table 4-1's Economic row: either state 'on the 730-hour paid-occupancy basis the same fleet spends $87,600/month for the same month (~241.9B input tokens at a 730-hour basis), yielding ~2.76M input tokens per $1 of spend', or relabel the 655K figure explicitly as 'whole-fleet spend paid for 730 h ÷ active-hours (173.3 h) input volume' and add 'not comparable with the 2.76M figure' in the same cell.

findings.evidence: on the wall-clock paid-occupancy basis (the sidebar's $87,600/mo — the fleet paid for all 730 h/mo, divided by the same 6.24M active-hours requests) it is ≈$14.04 per 1K, i.e. ~$0.014 per request. The 4.2× gap between $0.0033 and $0.014 is the duty cycle (730 ÷ 173.3 = 4.21), not a different fleet.
findings.issue: The 4.2× duty-cycle factor is applied to the $/request figure but the chapter elsewhere (Table 4-1 Economic row, and the sidebar table) presents $14.04 and $3.33 as two different 'per 1K req' numbers for the SAME 6-host fleet and the SAME 6.24M active-hours request volume. Only one of them ($3.33) is hour-matched end to end, which the sidebar's own 'Qualifier' column says ('hour-matched end to end ... — the smallest per-1K figure here'). But Table 4-1's Economic row puts '~$3.33' and '~$14.04' in adjacent positions with only the parenthetical numerator-hour basis, so a reader who lifts '$14.04 per 1K req' as the workload's unit cost — the more quotable number — gets a figure 4.2× the hour-matched cost. The book does not put a warning next to the $14.04 number that it is an artifact of paying 730 hours for 173.3 hours of work.
findings.fix_instruction: In Table 4-1's Economic row and in the sidebar table, append to the $14.04 and $49.13 figures an explicit qualifier in the same cell: 'wall-clock spend ÷ active-hours volume — hour-basis mismatch, not a per-request unit cost'. Add a one-line rule at the first use: 'Quote $3.33/1K (hour-matched) as the unit cost; the other figures are capacity-cost artifacts.'

findings.evidence: The canonical workload's operational constraint and SLA (this box: Multi-region deployment (active-active), 99.9% availability) state the requirement; the follow-on TCO and fleet arithmetic in Ch 16–17 prices a single-region deployment with N−1 single-host failover, not multi-region active-active. ... The canonical cost figures (Ch 16 $/1K req, Ch 17 host counts) therefore understate the cost of the canonical workload's own stated 99.9% availability requirement.
findings.issue: The book is explicit that its canonical TCO/fleet numbers underprice the canonical workload's own stated SLA, yet Table 4-1's Economic row (p. 79) and the Canonical Workload box (p. 83) still present the per-host monthly cost and the workload-level spend ranges (~$87.6K–$306.6K/mo at full utilization, ~$146K–$467K/mo on the 70% × 95% + N−1 policy fleet) without any pointer to this known underpricing in the same table cell. The gap is disclosed two pages earlier (p. 56) and then again on p. 83 as a separate note, but the Economic row itself — the row a reader lifts into a slide — carries no caveat.
findings.fix_instruction: Append to Table 4-1's Economic row and to the Canonical Workload box's 'Per-host monthly cost (reference)' row: 'Single-region, N−1 only; multi-region active-active for the 99.9% SLA is UNPRICED — these figures understate the workload's own availability requirement.'

findings.evidence: API list prices: ~$1.20 per 1M input tokens and ~$2.00 per 1M output tokens — mid-tier managed-API list price, 2026; [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] 2026 list-price snapshot, not a procured quote. Infrastructure: ≈ $20/hour for an 8×H100 host at $2.50/GPU-hr on-demand. Alternative bases: on the 730-hour paid-occupancy basis ... ~655K input tokens per $1 — a different hour-count denominator
findings.issue: Provenance drift across the two economics rows in the same table cell. The API prices are tagged [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] ('not a procured quote'), but the H100 price is introduced with the phrase 'illustrative 2026 cloud-price input' and no named vendor, no region, and no first-party citation — while the same $2.50/GPU-hr figure is carried elsewhere (Table 4-2, p. 89) as [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] 'dated price snapshot (2026 on-demand $2.50/GPU-hr × 8; not [1P] vendor spec, not a measured figure)'. The row's inline parenthetical '(canonical scenario)[ASSUMPTION]' appears only after the API-price sentence, leaving the H100 price tag ambiguous within the same cell. Table 4-1's table-level note says 'The only inline overrides are [1P] vendor hardware constants (Table 4-2) and [2°] externally benchmarked norms' — so a reader may expect the $2.50/GPU-hr to carry a [1P] tag, but it is explicitly not first-party.
findings.fix_instruction: Tag each price in the Economic row individually and identically: '$1.20/$2.00 per 1M [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] (2026 list snapshot, no named provider)'; '$2.50/GPU-hr on-demand [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] (2026 snapshot; not [1P], not a procured quote)'. Align the phrasing with Table 4-2's 'not [1P] vendor spec, not a measured figure' wording.

findings.evidence: We deliberately keep TWO named values, and the distinction matters: a planning round number of ~10 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08 s + decode ~7.5 s, rounded up to a comfortable planning figure) versus the derived model-execution service time of ~8.6 s (prefill 1.08 s + decode 7.5 s, without the retrieval/plumbing term) that the later fleet chapters use in Little's-law sizing.
findings.issue: The arithmetic stated here does not reproduce: retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08 s + decode ~7.5 s = ~8.70 s, which is described as 'rounded up to a comfortable planning figure' of ~10 s — a 15% round-up, and 'rounded up' understates it (8.70 → 10.00 is not rounding). Separately, the Canonical Workload box (p. 81) describes the same quantity as 'Mean request service time (planning) ~10 s [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] — an author-chosen round planning headline', while the same box's 'Execution occupancy' row derives from 'Wexec ≈ 8.6 s' and warns that ~10 s 'is also NOT the W used in any Little's-law occupancy computation'. Two service-time numbers for one workload, one of which the box itself says is not to be used, persist as the only 'mean request service time' row available.
findings.fix_instruction: Either drop the ~10 s planning figure or state it explicitly as a deliberate planning headroom multiplier: '~10 s = the ~8.7 s modelled total plus ~13% planning headroom — an author-chosen assumption, not a measurement'. In the Canonical Workload box, rename the row 'Mean request service time (planning headline, not used for occupancy)' so no reader can mistake it for Wexec.

findings.evidence: nhosts = ⌈50 rps × 8.6 s / 17 slots⌉ = ⌈430/17⌉ = ⌈25.29⌉ = 26 hosts (full utilization) and roughly ~37 hosts on the u-only screen at a 70% target utilization (⌈430/(17 × 0.7)⌉ = ⌈430/11.9⌉ = ⌈36.13⌉) — or 39 hosts before the spare, 40 under the book's provisioning policy
findings.issue: Re-derivation of the 10 rps/50 rps mini-case fleet screen: ⌈430/11.9⌉ = ⌈36.13⌉ = 37, but the book's own host-count form (stated at Ch. 17 Table 17-1 and quoted here) is total = ⌈N ÷ (ρ × u)⌉ with N = 26 full-utilization hosts, giving ⌈26 ÷ 0.665⌉ = ⌈39.10⌉ = 40 — the chapter acknowledges the two forms 'sit one host apart' at the intermediate stage. But the stated u-only comparison is wrong: the book's own u-only host-count form is ⌈N ÷ u⌉ = ⌈26 ÷ 0.70⌉ = ⌈37.14⌉ = 38, and the chapter does state this ('the host-count form gives ⌈26 ÷ 0.7⌉ = ⌈37.14⌉ = 38'). The real defect is that the occupancy form divides a request occupancy by a slots-per-host figure, which is not the book's stated canonical rule, yet the chapter calls it 'an instance of the canonical form, not as a competing rule' — while the two forms genuinely produce different host counts (37 vs 38; 39 vs 40) at the intermediate stages. The chapter's assertion that they 'agree at the final policy stage only' is fine, but calling the occupancy form 'the canonical form' contradicts Ch. 17's stated canonical rule.
findings.fix_instruction: Stop calling the occupancy form canonical. State both forms in Ch. 4 §4.8 as two equivalent-in-the-limit but distinct-at-rounding implementations of the Ch. 17 rule, and adopt the Ch. 17 host-count form (⌈N ÷ (u × ρ)⌉) as the single normative rule everywhere, with the occupancy form labeled as a cross-check that may differ by one host.

findings.evidence: Reference geometry — hidden dim (K/V width under full-MHA) 8,192 [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] every query head keeps its own K,V, so K/V width = hidden_dim = 8,192
findings.issue: The canonical model's geometry table asserts 8,192 as the hidden dim and states the K/V width equals the hidden dim 'under full-MHA', but it never states the head geometry. Ch. 7's sensitivity note (p. 124) derives the GQA variant as '64 query heads but only 8 KV-heads ... head_dim 128', and the per-rank fit note (p. 140) refers to 'the canonical 64-query-head full-MHA geometry', while Ch. 7's 3×H100 fit analysis (p. 122) states '64/3 = 21.3'. So the canonical model has 64 query heads of head_dim 128 (= 8,192) — consistent — but this is stated only in later chapters' asides and never appears in the canonical ledger that Table 4-2 claims is 'the authority for which is which'. A reader re-deriving any head-partition conclusion from Table 4-2 alone cannot do so.
findings.fix_instruction: Add two rows to Table 4-2: 'Query heads 64 [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]' and 'Head dim 128 [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]', and a note that full-MHA ⇒ 64 KV heads, so K/V width = 64 × 128 = 8,192 = hidden dim. Then reference Table 4-2 from Ch. 7's sensitivity and fit notes instead of re-deriving the geometry inline.

findings.evidence: Self-host — 21-host peak KV-screen fleet $155,816.93 ≈ $24.97 * 730 h/mo energy calendar capex amortized: 21 × ($350K ÷ 60 mo = $5,833.33 capex + $1,110.33 energy) = $145,816.93, + $10,000 fixed staff (Ch 16) — owned, not rented, so ~half the cloud 21-host line
findings.issue: Recomputation: 21 × 5,833.33 = 122,499.93; 21 × 1,110.33 = 23,316.93; sum = 145,816.86 ≈ $145,816.93 as stated ✓; plus $10,000 staff = $155,816.93 ✓. The arithmetic is correct. But the per-1K figure: 155,816.93 ÷ 6,240K = $24.97 ✓, and the stated 21-host cloud total $306,600 ÷ 6,240K = $49.13 ✓. The defect is the row's own claim 'owned, not rented, so ~half the cloud 21-host line': 155,816.93 ÷ 306,600 = 0.508, so '~half' is fair, yet the row sits in a table whose other rows are labelled 'Cloud, 6 hosts' and 'Cloud, 21 hosts always-on at peak' — and the cloud rows are compared against a self-host row whose numerator is a *730-hour* energy calendar while its denominator is a *173.3-hour* active volume, the same hour-basis mismatch flagged elsewhere in the chapter. The self-host row's Qualifier cell says '730 h/mo energy calendar' but the per-1K figure divides by an active-hours volume, so it carries the same defect the chapter warns about for the cloud rows without carrying the same warning.
findings.fix_instruction: Add to the self-host row's Qualifier cell: 'numerator paid over 730 h ÷ active-hours (173.3 h) volume — hour-basis mismatch; not a unit cost. The hour-matched self-host figure divides the 173.3-hour energy+capex+staff basis by the same 6.24M requests.'

findings.evidence: The walk-through makes the distinctions explicit: the ~100 active users are a population/activity measure, not a request-occupancy count; the ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak are declared traffic assumptions (scenario inputs), not derived from the user count; the ~86 / ~344 execution occupancy is derived from those arrival rates via Little's Law (L = λ × Wexec, Wexec ≈ 8.6 s).
findings.issue: Ambiguous referent: 'the ~86 / ~344 execution occupancy is derived from those arrival rates via Little's Law' — 'those arrival rates' has two possible antecedents in the immediately preceding clause ('the ~10 rps average / ~40 rps peak are declared traffic assumptions'), which is fine, but the sentence also uses 'execution occupancy' where the Canonical Workload box (p. 81) uses the row label 'Execution occupancy' with values '~86 requests at 10 rps (Wexec ≈ 8.6 s); ~344 at 40 rps'. Two names for the same quantity ('execution occupancy' vs 'occupancy' vs 'in-flight requests' vs 'resident slots') circulate across Ch. 4, Ch. 6 and Ch. 7, and Ch. 7's Fig 7.7 caption explicitly warns 'the arithmetic panel reads 'in-flight'; that quantity is the KV-resident slot count ... not the Little's-Law in-flight request count'. The four-term vocabulary for two distinct quantities is the book's largest remaining ambiguity risk.
findings.fix_instruction: Add a four-line terminology box in Ch. 4 §4.3 next to the operating-point table fixing the vocabulary: 'registered users (population)', 'active users (activity)', 'in-flight requests (Little's Law λ·W)', 'KV-resident sequences (slots)'. Then use exactly these four terms thereafter, and change Ch. 7 Fig 7.7's panel label from 'in-flight' to 'KV-resident slots' so the figure cannot be misread as the Little's-Law quantity.

findings.evidence: figure 4.1: Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions. Each arrow means the dimension constrains/informs the corresponding architectural choice — it is a heuristic influence, not a deterministic one-to-one mapping.
findings.issue: The figure's caption uses the word 'mapped' and the figure's title uses 'mapped', but the caption explicitly disclaims mapping ('not a deterministic one-to-one mapping') while the List of Figures (p. 9) records the title as 'Six-dimension workload characterization mapped to architectural decisions'. The chapter's own caption text enumerates a mapping that the figure's own framing denies, so a reader searching for 'the mapping from dimension to decision' will not find a mapping table, and Fig 4.1's role is ambiguous between a map and a lens.
findings.fix_instruction: Rename consistently to 'Six workload dimensions and the architectural decisions each one informs' and, in the caption, replace 'mapped to' with 'informing'. If a real mapping table is wanted, add one (dimension → decision → the chapter that prices it), which would also serve as the 'optimization decision map' pointer that Ch. 2 leaves unresolved.

findings.chapter: Ch. 4, Table 4-2 Note 1 vs. Preface 'Evidence boundary' (PDF p.17 / printed xi)
findings.evidence: Preface (PDF p.17, printed xi): 'Axis note: [ILLUSTRATIVE] is a provenance tag (Axis 1) only — a non-canonical worked example — and is never a measurement status; measurement status uses ANALYTICAL, SCENARIO-DERIVED, MODELED, MEASURED or UNMEASURED.' Table 4-2 Note 1 (PDF p.87, printed 67): 'Axis 3 measurement status — how far it has climbed the measurement hierarchy: ANALYTICAL / ILLUSTRATIVE / MODELED / MEASURED, or UNMEASURED.' Body usage follows the Preface (e.g. Fig 8.2 tag 'ANALYTICAL [DERIVED]', Ch. 2 'Analytical bound — not a benchmark').
findings.issue: The two definitions of the Axis-3 measurement-status enumeration contradict each other. Note 1 lists ILLUSTRATIVE as a measurement status, which the Preface explicitly forbids ('never a measurement status'), and Note 1 omits SCENARIO-DERIVED, which the Preface mandates. Since the evidence-label apparatus is the book's core discipline and Note 1 is the declared authority chapters refer back to, a reader applying Note 1 would tag scenario-derived values with a status the Preface bans.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite Note 1's Axis-3 enumeration to match the Preface set exactly: 'ANALYTICAL / SCENARIO-DERIVED / MODELED / MEASURED, or UNMEASURED', and add a cross-note that [ILLUSTRATIVE] is Axis-1-only (mirroring the Preface Axis note).

findings.evidence: Instances of the compressed form: PDF p.101 (printed 81) '(Ch 2 §1, developed in Ch 11)'; PDF p.96 (printed 76) '(canonical statement in Ch 7 §3, Fig 7.7)'; PDF p.105 (printed 85) 'from Ch 7 §3 and Ch 20'; PDF p.133 (printed 113) '(35% MFU, Ch 8 §3)'; PDF p.134 (printed 114) 'Ch 8 §3, Table 8-1' and '(Ch 8 §3; Ch 17)'. Declared convention (PDF p.20, printed xiii): 'Section cross-references use the § chapter.section form: a bare § N.M refers to chapter N, section M'.
findings.issue: Recurring nonconforming cross-reference form 'Ch N §M' instead of the declared '§ N.M' form. All six instances were verified to resolve to existing, on-topic targets (§2.1 terminology table; §7.3 worked example; §8.3.3–8.3.4 prefill screens), so this is a form-only defect, but it recurs across at least three chapters and undermines the convention the Preface states.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite the instances as '§ 2.1', '§ 7.3', '§ 8.3' respectively (six occurrences across printed pp. 76, 81, 85, 113, 114×2); run a global search for '§[0-9]' preceded by 'Ch' to catch any remaining instances in the unrendered chapters.

findings.evidence: PDF p. 77: "...Lexec = λ × Wexec ≈ 86 (~344 at 40 rps) is a separate derived quantity." PDF p. 85 (Printed Page 65): "...at the 40 rps peak volume of 24.96M requests/month the 21-host figure is ≈$12.28/1K..."
findings.issue: Internal contradiction regarding the time-basis for peak traffic volume. On PDF p. 85, the 'peak' traffic of 40 rps is extrapolated over a full 24×7 month (30 days) to yield 24.96M requests. However, PDF p. 77 states that the average 10 rps is 'over the active business-hours window (an 8-hour × 260-workday schedule)'. Applying 24×7 wall-clock scaling to peak rps while using 8×260 scaling for average rps is mathematically inconsistent and artificially depresses the peak cost-per-request by 3x.
findings.fix_instruction: Align the time-basis definitions. State clearly whether the peak 40 rps applies continuously 24/7 or only during the active business-hours window (which should yield ~8.32M peak requests/month, making the peak cost exactly $36.85/1K, identical to the 4x cost scaling relative to the baseline).

findings.chapter: Preface, Evidence Discipline; Ch. 4, Table 4-2 Note 1
findings.evidence: PDF 17: "Axis note: [ILLUSTRATIVE] is a provenance tag (Axis 1) only — a non-canonical worked example — and is never a measurement status; measurement status uses ANALYTICAL, SCENARIO-DERIVED, MODELED, MEASURED or UNMEASURED." PDF 90: "Axis 3 measurement status — how far it has climbed the measurement hierarchy: ANALYTICAL / ILLUSTRATIVE / MODELED / MEASURED, or UNMEASURED."
findings.issue: The allowed Axis 3 measurement-status vocabulary is inconsistent. The Preface says ILLUSTRATIVE is Axis 1 provenance only and explicitly must not be used as measurement status; Ch. 4 Note 1 lists ILLUSTRATIVE as an Axis 3 measurement status and omits SCENARIO-DERIVED.
findings.fix_instruction: Make the evidence taxonomy single-valued across the book. In Ch. 4 Note 1, replace ILLUSTRATIVE with SCENARIO-DERIVED and restore SCENARIO-DERIVED to the Axis 3 list, or amend the Preface/addenda if ILLUSTRATIVE was intentionally reclassified. Then sweep all table headers and figure captions that cite Axis 3.

findings.evidence: "Cost per request: At 10 rps, each request carries ~9,500 tokens (9,200 input + 300 output). At the per‑million rates, cost per request ≈ (9,200 × $1.20/1M) + (300 × $2.00/1M) = $0.01104 + $0.0006 = $0.01164 ≈ $0.012 per request per inference cycle (M = 1,000,000 per the book’s SI convention, so the 9.2 K input is 9,200 tokens, not 9.2). At 40 rps peak, cost scales linearly."
findings.issue: The sentence "At 40 rps peak, cost scales linearly" follows a per-request cost calculation and is ambiguous: per-request API cost remains about $0.012; aggregate cost rate scales with rps. As written, it can be read as claiming the per-request cost scales.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite the final sentence to distinguish the two quantities, e.g. "The per-request cost remains ~$0.012; aggregate cost per second or per month scales linearly with request rate."

findings.evidence: page 85 mini-case: "nhosts = ceil(430/17)=26 hosts (full utilization) and roughly ~37 hosts on u-only screen at 70% (ceil(430/11.9)=37)"; page 85 also gives host-count form ceil(26/0.665)=40 vs occupancy form 38.04=39
findings.issue: Two forms that must agree at occupancy step diverge: occupancy-form 430/(17*0.70*0.95)=38.04→39 vs host-count-form ceil(N/(u*ρ))=ceil(26/0.665)=39.10→40 differ by 1 host due to ceil before vs after division; MAX-of-all-screens enforcement not applied — text claims agreement while intermediate u-only stage shows 37 vs 38.
findings.fix_instruction: Add MAX-of-all-screens box and enforce consistent ceil placement: define N_full = ceil(load/C), then total = ceil(N_full / (u*ρ)); correct occupancy-only intermediate to 38 and state final policy-stage agreement vs intermediate-stage one-host delta explicitly.
